title: Work-efficient parallel directed reachability
formal:
Does directed single-source reachability admit nearly linear work and polylogarithmic depth simultaneously in the uniform randomized CREW PRAM model specified below? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists A_c,K_c,a_c,b_c,q_c\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall G\ \forall s\in V(G),
\]
\[
\Pr\!\left[\begin{array}{l}
A_c(G,s)\text{ terminates with the exact reachability indicator,}\\
W\le K_c(n+m)L^{a_c}\ \text{and}\ D\le K_cL^{b_c}
\end{array}\right]\ge1-n^{-c},
\]
where \(G\) ranges over every directed graph on the labeled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)? Here \(K_c\ge1\), \(a_c,b_c\ge0\) and \(q_c\ge3\) are integers independent of \(n,G,s\); \(A_c\) is one finite program independent of input size. The word length is \(q_cL\). The required event jointly bounds total work \(W\), depth \(D\), and correctness of the entire output on each fixed input. The confidence exponent is requested as a fixed constant before choosing the program. The one-vertex case has the prescribed output consisting of a single 1 and is omitted only to avoid a vacuous probability bound.
why: Directed reachability is a basic graph operation with a linear-work sequential solution. The unresolved issue is whether its dependencies can be processed in polylogarithmic parallel time while retaining nearly that work bound on every input. A resolution would determine whether a fundamental sequential graph task admits efficient use of many processors, rather than a speedup purchased with polynomially more computation.
definitions:
Graphs are unweighted and directed. Their edge sets satisfy \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}^{2}\); loops are allowed and repeated copies of an edge are absent. A vertex is reachable from \(s\) when there is a finite directed path from \(s\) to it, including the length-zero path. No assumption of strong connectivity, acyclicity, bounded diameter or a lower bound on \(m\) is imposed.

The input is an outgoing adjacency-array representation in shared read-only word memory. Cells 0, 1 and 2 contain \(n,m,s\). The next \(n+1\) cells contain offsets \(o_0,\ldots,o_n\), with \(0=o_0\le\cdots\le o_n=m\). The next \(m\) cells contain target labels \(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1}\). The outgoing neighbors of vertex \(v\) are exactly the distinct labels \(t_j\) for \(o_{v-1}\le j<o_v\). Neighbor order is arbitrary. The output occupies the next \(n\) cells, one word for each vertex in label order: its value must be 1 for a reachable vertex and 0 otherwise. Thus the answer is the entire exact set, represented by \(n\) Boolean values, and does not include distances or a transitive closure.

For the chosen program, words are unsigned \(w=q_cL\)-bit integers. Shared cells and processor identifiers are numbered from 0 to \(2^w-1\). Every processor has a fixed finite number of word registers and runs the same finite program, with its identifier available in a designated register. These register counts and the program may depend on \(c\), but not on the graph or its size. Noninput cells and all other registers initially contain zero. There is no advice, oracle, precomputed graph index or uncharged preprocessing. The polynomial address space is the only imposed working-space limit.

Execution is synchronous. One active processor executes one primitive instruction per round. Instructions read or write one shared cell by its word address; copy words; add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\); perform bitwise AND, OR, XOR or complement; shift a word left or logically right by an integer between 0 and \(w-1\); compare unsigned words; branch; or obtain one fresh unbiased random bit. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Instructions use a constant number of registers. Reads observe the memory at the beginning of the round, and writes commit at its end. Several processors may read one cell, but at most one processor may write a given cell in a round, even if competing writes would contain the same value. Input cells cannot be written. Programs must obey these CREW access rules on every execution.

To account explicitly for activation, only processor 0 starts active. A unit-cost fork instruction activates one previously unused processor with a specified identifier, a program entry label and a constant number of copied registers; it starts in the next round. Two simultaneous forks may not name the same processor. Halting a processor costs one instruction; halted or not-yet-activated processors do no work. All input-independent setup, processor activation, data movement, auxiliary graph construction and output writes count toward work. Work is the total number of executed primitive instructions, and depth is the number of synchronous rounds until all activated processors halt. Nontermination gives infinite depth and does not satisfy the success event. The fork convention makes processor initialization explicit and allows ordinary parallel scheduling with polylogarithmic overhead.

All random-bit instructions draw mutually independent fair bits; the probability is over these bits for each fixed input representation. The required probability concerns correct output and both resource bounds together, not three expectations or an average over graphs. On the exceptional event, the program may return an incorrect answer, exceed a resource bound or fail to terminate. The notation \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) and polylogarithmic depth in the motivating question is replaced by the explicit logarithmic powers and constants in the statement.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give directed single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(n+m)\) work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth with high probability. This entry uses the corrected fourth arXiv version of their FOCS 2019 paper.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak give \(\widetilde O(m)\) work and \((n^{\omega+o(1)}/m)^{1/(2\omega-2)}\) span for \(m\ge n\). Here \(\omega\) is the exponent used for parallel matrix multiplication. Their dense-graph bound is \(n^{0.136}\); this is not a polylogarithmic bound on arbitrary inputs.

Kogan and Parter claim polylogarithmic-depth single-source reachability with \(\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})\) work, where \(T\) is the number of ordered pairs in the reflexive transitive closure. The arXiv record reports FOCS 2026 acceptance. The claim concerns work in terms of \(T\), which need not be nearly linear in \(n+m\).

status_note: The full May 2026 source retains the sparse-graph work/depth frontier. The checked August 2026 preprint claims polylogarithmic depth with work in transitive-closure size, which can be quadratic even on a linear-size graph. Individual primary-source reading and a bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026 found no resolution of nearly linear input work with polylogarithmic depth on all directed graphs. This supports a dated source-open classification; it is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate or an independent verification of every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: The target concerns arbitrary directed inputs and the full reachable set from one source. Near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth must be achieved in the same execution. Neither a low-work algorithm with polynomial depth nor a fast parallel algorithm with polynomially excessive work meets that requirement.

The input parameter is \(n+m\), including isolated vertices. The cited papers sometimes assume \(m\ge n\) or absorb one implicit self-loop per vertex into \(m\). This card makes the additive vertex term explicit. For a directed path, \(m=n-1\), whereas the reflexive transitive closure contains \(n(n+1)/2\) ordered pairs; a bound in closure size can therefore be much larger than a bound in input size.

The sources use the standard work/depth terminology but do not fully specify shared-memory write conflicts, word instructions or input layout. This card retains its previously selected CREW convention and makes word size, adjacency arrays, exact output, processor activation and the joint high-probability event explicit editorial model choices. It permits a program selected for each fixed confidence exponent; the program is uniform over input sizes. These details are not quotations of a particular source model.

The May 2026 full version explicitly identifies improving the sparse-graph regime as open. The August result gives polylogarithmic depth with work parameterized by \(T=|TC(G)|\), where \(TC(G)=\{(u,v):v\text{ is reachable from }u\}\). Since \(T\) may be quadratic on a sparse graph, that theorem does not provide the nearly linear input-work guarantee asked for here.

answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified algorithm-existence statement or its negation in the specified model. A positive answer must provide the uniform program witnesses and prove the joint correctness, work and depth guarantee on every admissible graph, source and adjacency-array ordering for every fixed confidence exponent. A negative answer must refute that entire existence statement without an additional unproved complexity assumption. A result restricted to a class of graphs, a particular representation of auxiliary information, or work measured by transitive-closure size does not establish either answer unless it entails the full statement.

Explicitly, a negative answer establishes an integer \(c\ge1\) such that for every legal finite program and every proposed integer constants \(K\ge1\), \(a,b\ge0\), \(q\ge3\), there are \(n\ge2\), a valid graph, source and adjacency-array ordering for which the joint probability in the formal statement is strictly below \(1-n^{-c}\). A legal program obeys the stated word and CREW rules on all executions. The failing instance may depend on the candidate program and constants.

importance.reason: Combining near-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for directed reachability would resolve a major barrier in efficient parallel graph algorithms.

sentences: Given a directed graph and a source, the task is to mark exactly all vertices reachable from that source.
The question asks for a uniform randomized CREW parallel algorithm with nearly linear total work in the input size and polylogarithmic depth on every input.
Correctness of the complete output and both resource bounds must hold together with high probability for each fixed graph.
The 2026 density improvement retains polynomial depth, while the August polylogarithmic-depth result measures work by a potentially quadratic transitive closure.
A complete Lean proof must decide whether the two desired resource guarantees can be achieved simultaneously in the specified model.
